hints: Think about where the change from giant structures to simple molecules happens in Period 3, Na to S.
Use the maximum oxidation number equal to the group number to work out the formulae of oxides with $\text{O}^{2-}$ and chlorides with $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
Remember that P shows its maximum +5 state in both its oxide and chloride, while S in $\text{SCl}_{2}$ is an exception with a lower state.
walkthrough:
Sort metals from non-metals**
Picture Period 3. Na, Mg and Al are metals, so each element has metallic bonding with positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Si, P and S are non-metals with covalent structures. So Mg and Al are metallic and Si is covalent.

Build the oxide formulae**
Oxygen is $\text{O}^{2-}$ in oxides. Balance the Period 3 oxidation state, which is the group number: Na +1 gives $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, Mg +2 gives $\text{MgO}$, Al +3 gives $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, Si +4 gives $\text{SiO}_{2}$. P is already given as $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$.

Build the chloride formulae**
Chlorine is $\text{Cl}^{-}$ in chlorides. Again use the maximum oxidation state: Al +3 gives $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, Si +4 gives $\text{SiCl}_{4}$, P +5 gives $\text{PCl}_{5}$. NaCl and $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ fit the same rule.

Final answer: Bonding: Mg metallic, Al metallic, Si covalent.
Oxides: $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, $\text{SiO}_{2}$.
Chlorides: $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$, $\text{PCl}_{5}$.

hints: Count outer electrons first: S has 6 and each Cl has 7, so share one pair with each Cl to give all atoms a full octet.
walkthrough:
Draw a bent $\text{SCl}_{2}$ molecule**
Put S in the middle with a Cl on each side. S shares one pair of electrons with each Cl, so there are two $\text{S-Cl}$ single covalent bonds. That uses 2 of the 6 outer electrons of S. The remaining 4 electrons on S stay as 2 lone pairs. Each Cl started with 7 outer electrons, shares 1, so each Cl keeps 6 electrons as 3 lone pairs. Show S electrons as crosses and Cl electrons as dots, or vice versa, with all pairs in the overlap or on the atoms.
Final answer: S central with 2 shared pairs (one to each Cl) and 2 lone pairs on S; each Cl with 1 shared pair and 3 lone pairs. Outer electrons only, with dots and crosses to distinguish origin.

hints: Use the sign of $\Delta H = -40.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to decide whether products finish higher or lower than reactants.
Recall that $E_{a}$ is measured from reactants up to the top of the hump, while $\Delta H$ is measured from reactants to products.
walkthrough:
Place products below reactants**
A negative $\Delta H$ means exothermic, so energy is released. Draw the curve rising from the $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(l) + \text{Cl}_{2}(g)$ level to a hump and then falling to a lower $2\text{SCl}_{2}(l)$ level.

Label the two energy gaps**
$E_{a}$ is the climb you need to start the reaction, so draw a double arrow from the reactant level up to the top of the hump. $\Delta H$ is the overall change, so draw a double arrow from the reactant level down to the product level and label it $\Delta H = -40.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: Curve starting at $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(l) + \text{Cl}_{2}(g)$, rising to a peak then falling to $2\text{SCl}_{2}(l)$ at a lower energy level. $E_{a}$ labelled from reactants to peak, $\Delta H$ labelled from reactants down to products.

hints: Recall which Period 3 element has a giant covalent lattice and therefore the very highest melting point.
walkthrough:
Sketch rise, peak, then sharp fall**
Start low at Na, rise to Mg, rise a little more to Al, then rise to a clear peak at Si. After Si drop steeply down to P, then go up slightly to S. Si must be the highest point and P and S must be low, because they are simple molecules.
Final answer: Sketch rises from Na to Mg to Al to a maximum at Si, then falls sharply to P and rises slightly to S, with P and S well below Na, Mg, Al.

hints: Compare Na, Mg and Al by thinking about ion charge and number of delocalised electrons pulling on the lattice.
Think about what must be broken to melt Si compared with melting a metal.
Compare $\text{P}_{4}$ and $\text{S}_{8}$ as simple molecules by thinking about size of electron cloud and strength of temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
Explain Na to Al rising**
Melting a metal means loosening the attraction between positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. From Na to Al the ion charge rises from +1 to +3 and the number of delocalised electrons per atom rises from 1 to 3, while ions get smaller. That stronger attraction needs more heat, so melting point rises Na < Mg < Al.

Explain why Si is the peak**
Si is a giant covalent lattice with strong $\text{Si-Si}$ covalent bonds in three dimensions. To melt it you must break these strong bonds, which takes far more energy than loosening metallic bonds. That is why Si sits at the top of the graph.

Explain P and S as low and S higher than P**
P exists as $\text{P}_{4}$ and S as $\text{S}_{8}$ molecules. Melting does not break covalent bonds inside the molecules, it only overcomes weak induced dipole-dipole forces between molecules, so melting points are low. $\text{S}_{8}$ is larger with more electrons than $\text{P}_{4}$, so it has stronger temporary dipoles and stronger forces, giving S a higher melting point than P.

Final answer: Na < Mg < Al due to increasing strength of metallic bonding with higher ion charge and more delocalised electrons giving stronger attraction to positive ions.
Si has highest melting point as giant covalent, strong covalent bonds must be broken, requiring most energy.
P and S are simple molecules with weak induced dipole-dipole forces so low melting points; $\text{S}_{8}$ has stronger forces than $\text{P}_{4}$ so S melts higher than P.

hints: Remember that $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ is an acidic oxide that reacts fully with water to give phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$.
walkthrough:
Balance P then H and O**
$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ needs 4 $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ to balance P. That gives 12 H on the right, so you need $6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ on the left. Check O: $10 + 6 = 16$ on the left, $4 \times 4 = 16$ on the right. The balanced equation is $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$.

hints: Think about what happens when $\text{SO}_{2}$ dissolves in rain water and is oxidised in the air.
Link increased acidity to one clear effect on lakes, trees, buildings or health.
walkthrough:
Name acid rain**
$\text{SO}_{2}$ dissolves in water in the atmosphere and is oxidised to sulfuric acid, so rain becomes more acidic. This is acid rain.

Give one explained consequence**
Extra $\text{H}^{+}$ lowers the pH of rivers, lakes and soil. That kills fish and other aquatic life, damages leaves and roots of trees and crops, leaches toxic $\text{Al}^{3+}$ from soil into water, and attacks carbonate stone so buildings and statues weather and erode.

Final answer: Causes acid rain.
Lowers pH of lakes / rivers / soil, killing aquatic life / damaging trees / crops, or erodes buildings / statues, or leaches $\text{Al}^{3+}$ from soil.

hints: Write the definition of first ionisation energy as removal of one electron to form a $1+$ ion.
Look at the Data Booklet values and spot the two places where the value falls instead of rising.
For Mg to Al, compare removal from a 3s orbital with removal from a 3p orbital.
For P to S, think about what is different about the 3p electrons in S where one orbital contains a pair.
walkthrough:
Define first ionisation energy**
Keep it precise: $\text{X}(g) \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}(g) + e^{-}$. It is the energy to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous $1+$ ions.

Identify the two dips**
The general rise is due to increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding. The two exceptions are Mg to Al where the value falls, and P to S where the value falls.

Explain Mg to Al**
Mg loses a 3s electron: $[Ne]3s^{2}$. Al loses a 3p electron: $[Ne]3s^{2}3p^{1}$. The 3p electron is higher in energy, on average further from the nucleus and more shielded by the 3s electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it. Hence Al has a lower first ionisation energy than Mg.

Explain P to S**
P is $[Ne]3s^{2}3p^{3}$ with three unpaired p electrons in separate orbitals. S is $[Ne]3s^{2}3p^{4}$ with one pair in the same orbital. The two electrons sharing one orbital repel each other, making one of them easier to remove. Hence S has a lower first ionisation energy than P.

Final answer: First ionisation energy: removal of one electron from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous $1+$ ions.
Pairs: Mg and Al, P and S.
Al lower than Mg because outer electron in 3p is higher in energy / further from nucleus / more shielded than 3s, so removed more easily.
S lower than P because paired electrons in same 3p orbital repel, so electron removed more easily.
